newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's "Mr Yen" could face new challenge.
newsitem.headline: Japan's "Mr Yen" could face new challenge.

text.p: Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara is a rarity in Japan -- a nail that sticks up but has not been hammered down.

The controversial, outspoken Sakakibara, dubbed "Mr Yen" for his ability to sway currency markets with a single comment, could face a new challenge if, as many expect, he's promoted to a post as Japan's foremost financial diplomat.
Sakakibara is the favoured candidate to take over as vice finance minister for international affairs, a step up after two years as director of the ministry's International Finance Bureau.

Finance Ministry (MOF) officials say that no formal decision is likely until mid-July and speculation persists that Sakakibara's detractors will succeed in keeping Takatoshi Kato as vice minister for an unusual third year.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Friday after returning from China that no decisions had been made on any personnel issues.
But if Kato -- a soft-spoken man inclined to cautious comments -- steps down, most MOF watchers expect Sakakibara to replace him.

Sakakibara has been credited with spearheading a drive to counter the yen's steep rise in 1995 with financial market liberalisation steps and was instrumental in revising foreign exchange laws as a step toward Tokyo's "Big Bang" reforms.
He also played a key role in forging pacts with Asian nations to stabilise regional currencies.
"Japan faced a real economic emergency (in spring 1995) when the yen was around 80 (to the dollar) and the stock market was falling," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan.
Sakakibara's aggressive personality and some alleged missteps in the past won him many enemies within the ministry, but some say the tide has shifted since then.

"His support in the ministry is much more broad-based than two years ago. Then, he was odd man out for his controversial views and controversial ways of doing things. But success has proven him right," Koll said.
Sakakibara had already earned a reputation as a tough negotiator in U.S.-Japan talks on deregulation of Japan's insurance market when he took up his current post in June 1995.

A fluent English-speaker who earned a doctorate at the University of Michigan after graduating from the prestigious University of Tokyo, Sakakibara's economic views also earned him a place among a circle of intellectuals and bureaucrats dubbed by some "Japan's new nationalists."

Those views were laid out in his book, "Beyond Capitalism," in which he argued that Japan has a distinctive non-capitalist market economy which might be a better guide for developing nations than the U.S. model. Japanese firms, he said, compete in more or less free markets but the system places people above profits and mere efficiency.

Despite his support for Tokyo's "Big Bang" reforms aimed at introducing more competition into Japan's long-protected financial sector, Sakakibara insists Japan can cling to a core of traditional values.
"With regard to financial and information technology, we must catch up with Europe and the United States," he was quoted as saying in a magazine interview earlier this year.
"But it is quite possible to remain Japanese while incorporating these, and I think ultimately the Japanese spirit of cooperation and harmony is very important," he said.

Sakakibara's penchant for speaking out and standing up for for his own views could stand him in good stead should he assume the top international post, as would his close ties with U.S. and Asian counterparts.
"It would be good to have someone with a clear vision of where he wants to go," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia.
"There are real decisions to be made and he's a guy who is not afraid to make them," he said.
But a more senior job for Sakakibara could also bring more exchange rate volatility given his brashness.
"The higher up you go in the hierarchy the greater risk loquaciousness is," Feldman said. "But markets are helped if they know where they're going."
